Mario Party 4 PowerPC Edition
=============================
Version 0.9.6


WHAT THIS IS

A native PowerPC port of Mario Party 4, built from the mariopartyrd
decompilation and running as a real Mac OS X application on a Power Mac G4.
This is not an emulator: the game's own C code is compiled for the G4's
processor, its 99 code modules load as native bundles, and the GameCube's
GX graphics commands are translated into OpenGL 1.3 for the Radeon 9000
as the game produces them, with the transform and lighting on the card's
vertex unit and the audio mixed on the CPU.  A board plays at the console's
speed with the picture at 30 frames a second.

Drag the application into your Applications folder.


WHAT IT NEEDS

The game checks the machine every time it starts, before the window opens,
and says what it found in the window's title and on the log.

Minimum: a PowerPC G4 Mac running Mac OS X 10.4 or later, 256 MB of
memory, and a graphics card of the Radeon 9000 class or better -- four or
more texture units with ATI's combiner extensions -- on which the game
runs, slower than a console on anything under 800 MHz.

Recommended: a dual 1 GHz G4 (or better) with a 64 MB Radeon 9000 or
better and Mac OS X 10.5.  That is the machine the port was built on, where
it runs at console speed.

By card, as far as the drivers' extension lists say (only the first line
has been run on real hardware):

    ATI Radeon 9000 / 9000 Pro, 64 MB         runs at full speed (the
    (Power Mac G4 2002-03)                    reference card)
    ATI Radeon 9000 / 9200 / Mobility 9200,   runs; the texture cache is
    32 MB (eMac 2004, iBook G4, PowerBook     sized down to the card, and
    12"/15" 2003)                             a first run says so
    ATI Radeon 9600 / 9700 / 9800 and their   expected to run at full
    Mobility versions (PowerBook G4 2004+,    speed; not yet tried
    Power Mac G4 / G5)
    NVIDIA GeForce FX 5200 / 6600             unknown: it depends on whether
                                              Apple's driver lists the ATI
                                              combiner extension
    NVIDIA GeForce4 MX / GeForce2 MX,         refused: two or three texture
    ATI Radeon 7500 / 7000 / Rage 128         units cannot draw the picture

A machine below the minimum gets a dialog saying why, and the game does not
start.  A machine that runs but below what the port was built for gets that
dialog once, then runs.  An Intel Mac is refused: the PowerPC binary does run
under Rosetta, but slowly and with a different picture, and it is not what
this is built for.

SDL2 is inside the application; there is nothing else to install.


YOU BRING THE DISC IMAGE

No game data is included.  You need your own dump of your Mario Party 4 disc
-- the USA release, revision 1 (game id GMPE01) -- as a .iso; a trimmed NKit
.iso is fine, and so is a folder holding the disc's extracted files/ tree.

The first time you open the game it asks for that file with a standard Open
dialog, checks that it is the right disc, and remembers where it is.  You are
not asked again.  If you move the image the game asks once more; to point it
at a different image, move the old one out of the way or delete the `image`
line from the config file (see WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE).

Two ways to skip the dialog altogether: put the .iso in a folder named
MarioParty4 in your home folder (~/MarioParty4/), where the game looks
before asking; or run it from the Terminal with --image and the path.


THE SCREEN

A first run comes up fullscreen: the 640x480 picture scaled to the largest
4:3 rectangle that fits your display, letterboxed black at the sides, and the
choice is remembered.  For a window instead, run it once from the Terminal:

    open -a "Mario Party 4" --args --windowed

or change `fullscreen = 1` to `fullscreen = 0` in the config file.  Either is
remembered from then on; --fullscreen puts it back.


LOADING

Loading a minigame or a board is a read of your disc image, and on a slow
or busy disk that read can hold the game for half a second or more (the
picture and the music pause together; the game then catches up).  Two things
in this version make those reads come from memory instead.  Neither changes
what the game does or when: the game reads the same bytes at the same
moment, and only where they come from is different.

    The read-ahead.  The moment the roulette stops on a minigame -- several
    seconds before the game loads it -- the module and its data are read
    into the system's file cache in the background, so the game's own read
    finds them there.  The same for the board at the results screen and for
    the board set at the mode select.  On a two-processor Mac this runs on
    the second processor; on a single processor it runs in small pieces in
    the idle time between frames, and not at all when there is none.  It is
    on for every machine; --noprefetch turns it off.

    The resident set.  The files every game reads -- the board's data, the
    instruction and results screens', the four characters' models and the
    sound banks -- are read once and kept in the game's own memory, and
    answered from there for the rest of the run; a minigame's files join
    the set as they are read ahead and the least recently used leave when
    it is full.  Its size is decided by the machine check from the memory
    installed: none under 768 MB, 128 MB with 1 GB, 256 MB with 1.5 GB or
    more, and never so much that the system and the game have less than
    about 600 MB between them.  --resident 0 turns it off; --resident 64
    (any number of megabytes) sets it by hand.  Both decisions are on the
    log's "machine:" lines and in --defaults.

On the machine this was built on -- a dual 1 GHz Power Mac with 1.5 GB --
the two together turn a twenty-turn board's 319 MB of disc reading into
about 110 MB held in memory and one read from the disk, and a cold walk
through six minigames goes from thirty-odd reads over a tenth of a second
(three of them long enough to drop a second of game time) to three or
four.  The game uses about 110 MB more memory with the set than without.

Nothing is copied anywhere: the set is built from your own disc image at
every start and is gone when the game quits.


CONTROLS

Keyboard (always active, beside a pad too)

    Arrow keys / WASD       control stick
    I K J L                 C stick
    T G F H                 D-pad up / down / left / right
    Z  X  C  V              A  B  X  Y
    Q  E                    L  R
    Shift or Tab            Z
    Return                  Start (the game's own pause, in a minigame)
    F5 (or F12)             screenshot onto the Desktop, as a PNG named by
                            the frame (Mac OS X 10.5 gives F12 to Dashboard
                            unless you change that in System Preferences)
    Esc                     quit
    Cmd+Q                   quit

Game pads: Xbox One controllers over USB are driven directly (no driver
to install); any other pad SDL recognises works through its own mapping.
Every pad plugged in before the game starts gets a port, in order: the
Xbox One pads first, then the others, up to four.  With one pad the
keyboard works beside it as player 1; to make the keyboard a controller
of its own -- player 2 on the keys, say -- run once from the Terminal:

    open -a "Mario Party 4" --args --kbport 2

(A port that has a controller makes that player human on the character
select, as on a console; players without one are computer players.  The
switch is not remembered: it is for the run it is given to.)

    Left stick              control stick
    Right stick             C stick
    A B X Y                 A B X Y
    LT / RT                 L / R (analogue, with the click near the end)
    LB                      Z
    Menu (Start)            Start
    D-pad                   D-pad

Rumble works on a pad that has it.

Quitting -- Esc, Cmd-Q or the window's close button -- goes through the
game's own reset, as the console's Reset button does: the game fades, the
memory card is written, and the application leaves.  There is no separate
pause outside the game's own (Start, in a minigame).

For a bug report:  open -a "Mario Party 4" --args --defaults   prints every
setting the game would run with;  --keys  prints the table above.  The log
of the last run is in the folder below.


WHERE YOUR THINGS LIVE

    ~/Library/Application Support/MarioParty4/
        memcard-slot-a.raw    the memory card (a 59-block card image, the
                              same layout Dolphin uses, so a save moves
                              either way)
        config                the disc image's path, the fullscreen choice
        MarioParty4.log       the log of the last run

Deleting the folder loses your save file, so that is the folder to back up.
The disc image stays wherever you keep it.


WHAT IS NOT QUITE RIGHT YET

Every minigame has been compared against the real game frame by frame,
and the author of this package then went through every frame by hand
(37 notes: shadows, water, black where the console draws, and single
games); what is left that a player can see:

    Mario Medley        the pool's light ripple is a flat tint, and the
                        water is grey-green where the console's is blue
    Makin' Waves        the pool has a flat tint where the console
                        ripples it
    Cheep Cheep Sweep   the pond is clear where the console's reflects
                        the sky (the same missing ripple)
    Goomba's Chip Flip  the felt is black on the Radeon 9000 (the same
                        picture is green on an Intel card)

The ripple of those three pools is a warp the card's fixed pipeline
cannot do; a fragment-program path for it is in this build behind
--tfs, and stays off because the Radeon's Leopard driver draws two of
the three pools wrong through it (the notes say how far it got).

The character select screen runs at about 23 frames a second on the
reference machine (the board and most minigames run at the 30 cap).
This version sends the card 7% fewer drawing commands on that screen
and 1% fewer on the title, by not starting a new batch of triangles
when the game re-sends a setting it already had; the picture is
identical to the last version's, frame for frame, and the frame rate
moves by less than the difference between two runs of the same walk.
Intro movies are skipped.  The game's memory card is one card in slot A;
slot B is always empty.  A second controller works (checked with a pad on
port 1 and the keyboard standing in as player 2); three and four are
wired the same way but untested, there being one pad in the house.


LICENCE AND CREDITS

The game is the property of its rightsholders.  Nothing in this package
contains any of its data: you supply your own disc image, and the source
repository has never contained one.

The game's code comes from the mariopartyrd/marioparty4 decompilation,
compiled as is.  The MusyX audio library is Axiomatic Data Laboratories'
reimplementation (MIT).  SDL2 is under the zlib licence.  The licence texts
are in the Licences folder beside this file, with a note on the port layer
itself.

This package is built for one person's own Power Mac and is not for
redistribution.
